place: A slow lowland river with a muddy launch bank where a freshly hollowed dugout, cut from a green log, waits to be tried.
lines: I push the dugout into the water and climb in
I paddle out toward the middle of the river
outcome: The dugout floats, but because the wood is green it is dense and heavy, so the hull sits low with little freeboard from the start. Paddling out works, but leaning to either side brings water right up to the gunwale. Over the following days in the sun the wood loses some of the water it was cut with and rides a little higher, though never as high as a boat carved from dry timber.

numbers: how much force is needed to slide it over the mud
how low it sits, from the wood's density and the hull's shape

effects: moves canoe to middle of river
numbers: how fast it travels for the effort spent
how much water comes over the side for a given lean
how many days it takes to dry, how much lighter it gets

latent: a hairline crack along the log's grain, hidden under the bark, that will open into a leak later
state_after: dugout canoe: afloat, low in the water, slowly drying and lightening
stress: buoyancy follows from a specific log's density and hull volume, not from 'canoes' being a stable category of thing
temptation: a rule that says dugout canoes always tip when you lean, instead of computing freeboard from weight and hull shape

place: A boatwright's landing where a plank boat with open, gapped seams sits pulled half out of the river.
lines: I pack moss into the gaps between the planks
I melt pitch over a fire and smear it along the seams
I push the boat back into the water
outcome: The moss and pitch close the gaps and the boat floats dry at first, exactly as caulking should. But the pitch is brittle once it cools, and the boat flexes slightly every time it rocks on the current, so over the following days a seam along one plank works the coating loose. The boat starts taking on a slow trickle of water at that one seam, well before anyone would call it damaged.

numbers: how much moss fills the gaps
how long and how hot it must be melted
how much pitch is needed to cover the seams
how much water stays out at first
how many days before the pitch cracks, how much water gets in per day after

latent: a plank with tighter, oilier grain that never fully took the pitch, hidden beneath the smooth coat
state_after: plank boat: afloat, one seam cracking, taking on a slow leak
stress: a seal fails from material fatigue and flexing over time, not from a fixed leak-chance rolled once at launch
temptation: a rule that says caulked boats never leak until a set number of days have passed

place: A river crossing where a flat ferry raft carries goods and passengers between two landings on a moderate current.
lines: I load the sacks of grain onto the ferry
I wave the last two passengers aboard
I push off from the landing
outcome: Each sack and each passenger sinks the ferry a little further, and by the time it pushes off there is barely a hand's width of freeboard left. Mid-river, chop from the current starts washing over the low side faster than a passenger can bail it out, and the raft settles lower still. Depending on how much more comes aboard, it either limps to the far bank leaking badly or swamps outright, dumping cargo over the side.

numbers: how much freeboard is lost per sack
how much more it sinks per passenger
how much water comes aboard per wave, from freeboard
how fast bailing removes water compared to how fast it comes in

effects: transfers sacks of grain from ferry raft to river water
numbers: how much cargo is lost, whether it swamps fully or barely reaches the bank

latent: a passenger who cannot swim, unmentioned until the raft starts going under
state_after: ferry raft: swamped, drifting, part of its cargo gone
sacks of grain: soaked, some sunk
stress: load determines freeboard, and freeboard determines how much each wave adds, compounding rather than a single overload check
temptation: a rule that says ferries capsize once more than a fixed number of units are aboard

place: A narrow stretch where the current runs fast over a stony riverbed, and a punt boat is being poled upstream against it.
lines: I plant the pole against the riverbed and push
I lift the pole and plant it again further along
outcome: Poling normally walks the boat upstream a step at a time, but here the pole's foot wedges into a gap between two stones on the bed. While the player wrestles it free, the current has nothing holding the boat's line and swings it broadside, and by the time the pole comes loose the boat has drifted back downstream past where the push began.

numbers: how far it advances per push
how likely a gap catches the pole's foot
how fast it turns broadside once unheld
how long it takes to free
how far it drifts back while the pole is stuck

latent: the same gap between stones has snagged other poles before, its edges already worn smooth
state_after: punt boat: drifted downstream of the starting point
pole: scraped and muddy at the foot
stress: steerage is lost the instant the pole is committed to the bed and not free to correct the boat's line
temptation: a rule that says poling upstream always advances the boat by one fixed step per push

place: A landing stage where a rowboat is tied to a rough wooden piling, the current tugging steadily at the line day and night.
lines: I loop the rope twice around the piling and tie it off
outcome: The knot holds perfectly well; nothing about the tying is wrong. But the rope rubs against the piling's rough edge with every small surge of current, and the same few inches of fiber take all the wear. Over several days those fibers fray through, and the rope finally parts on its own with nobody there to see it, leaving the rowboat to drift off and be found downstream, or not found at all.

numbers: how much force the current puts on the line
how many days of rubbing it takes to fray through at one spot
how much tension the frayed spot can still take before parting
how far and how fast it drifts before anyone notices

latent: a second, looser wrap of old rope on the piling that nobody thought to use as a backup line
state_after: rowboat: adrift downstream, unattended
rope: parted, one frayed end still knotted to the piling
stress: mooring failure comes from sustained wear at a single contact point, not a random break rolled after some fixed number of days
temptation: a rule that says ropes break after a set number of days tied up, regardless of what they rub against

place: A fishing stretch of open current where an old branch lies fully submerged and invisible from the surface.
lines: I cast the net out across the current
I let it sink on its weights
I start hauling it back in
outcome: The net spreads, sinks on its weights as intended, and starts to gather fish. But its trailing edge drapes over the hidden branch and hooks fast on it, and hauling only pulls the mesh tighter against the snag instead of freeing it. The net tears where it is stressed hardest, most of the catch slips out through the gap, and the caught corner has to be cut away and left on the branch.

numbers: how far it spreads on the cast
how fast it sinks
how much force it takes before the mesh gives

effects: transfers fish from fishing net to river water
numbers: how many fish escape through the tear
how much net is abandoned on the branch

latent: the sunken branch has snagged other nets before, still wrapped in rotted cord from past losses
state_after: fishing net: torn, missing a corner
sunken branch: wrapped in old net cord
fish: mostly escaped downstream
stress: an unseen obstacle below the surface causes a gear loss that is only ever discovered by its effect, never announced in advance
temptation: a rule that names this stretch of river as the place nets always snag

place: A shallow bend where a weir of stakes and wattle fencing spans part of the river to funnel fish into a basket trap.
lines: I check the fish trap at the weir
I pull the caught branches and reeds out from between the stakes
outcome: Over the days between visits, the weir catches drifting branches and mats of reeds against its upstream face just as readily as it catches fish. The blockage backs the water up and slows the flow through the trap, so fewer fish are carried into the basket and the water pools noticeably higher on the upstream side. Clearing the debris restores the flow and the catch, but the same thing starts building again with the next rise in the current.

numbers: how much debris arrives per day
how much the water rises behind the weir
how much the flow through the trap drops
how many fewer fish enter the trap
how long clearing takes

latent: a stake near the base already loosened by the pressure of the trapped debris behind it
state_after: fish weir: cleared and flowing again, one stake loose at the base
river water: settling back toward its normal level upstream
stress: the weir's own working principle, catching things in the current, works against it by catching debris as readily as fish
temptation: a rule that says weirs need clearing every fixed number of days regardless of how much debris the river is carrying

place: A mill built over a fast side-channel of the river, its water wheel turning steadily to drive the grindstone.
outcome: A branch swept down the side-channel wedges between the wheel's paddles and its housing, and the wheel jams solid with nobody nearby to see it happen. The current keeps pushing on the stopped wheel, straining the axle, and the strain concentrates on the weakest part of the gearing until a wooden tooth cracks. The mill goes quiet, and only the sudden silence tells the miller something is wrong.

numbers: how often the channel carries something this size
how much force builds against the jam over time
how much strain the tooth can take before it fails
how long before the silence is noticed

latent: the branch snapped off a tree upstream during last week's wind, entirely unrelated to anything happening at the mill
state_after: water wheel: jammed, motionless, branch still wedged in the paddles
gear tooth: cracked
grindstone: stopped
stress: an object's arrival is independent of anyone's action, and mechanical strain accumulates against a fixed obstruction until something gives
temptation: a rule that says water wheels jam on a fixed schedule rather than from a specific branch arriving and wedging

place: The dug channel, or mill race, that feeds a water wheel from the main river, during a dry stretch when the river itself is running low.
outcome: With the main river low, less water enters the race and the current through it slows. Slower water can no longer sweep along the fine silt it used to carry straight through, so the silt settles on the race's bed, making it shallower still, which slows the current further in turn. Over the following weeks the wheel gets less water and less push, and the grinding grows steadily weaker until someone dredges the race back out.

because: patient is fed by the river
numbers: how much the flow through the race drops
how much silt settles per day at this flow
how much further the flow drops once shallower
how much the grinding output falls over the weeks

latent: a buried stone in the race bed that will catch and turn a dredging shovel once someone tries to clear it
state_after: mill race: shallow, half silted, flowing weakly
water wheel: turning slowly, grinding little
stress: a feedback loop where reduced flow causes silting, which further reduces flow, compounding gradually rather than a single one-shot event
temptation: a rule that says mill races silt up after a fixed number of dry days

place: A shallow, gravelly stretch of bank where woven cloth is beaten and trodden in the current to clean and full it.
lines: I weight the cloth down with flat stones and start treading it in the shallows
I lift a corner to see how it's coming along
outcome: Treading works the cloth against the gravel exactly as fulling should, loosening dirt and tightening the weave. But the current keeps tugging at whatever isn't weighted down, and when a stone slips off a wet corner the current catches that loose end and carries a length of it downstream before the player can grab it back, leaving the cloth torn and shorter than it was.

numbers: how long treading takes to full it
how much force the current puts on any unweighted edge
how likely the weighting slips loose while treading
how far it travels before it's grabbed or lost
how much is recovered against how much tears off

latent: a weak spot in the weave from an old mend, exactly where the cloth gives way under the current's pull
state_after: woven cloth: cleaner and tighter-woven, but torn and shorter
flat stones: scattered loose in the shallows
stress: the same current that fulls the cloth by working it against the gravel is what steals it the moment its grip is lost
temptation: a rule that says fulling cloth in a river always damages it by some fixed amount

place: A shallow ford where a cart track crosses the river, normally no deeper than a knee, the day after heavy rain fell upstream.
lines: I lead the ox and cart down to the ford and start across
outcome: The ford that was easy yesterday is higher and faster today from rain that fell upstream overnight. Partway across, the water reaches the cart bed and pushes sideways against the wheels, and when the ox misjudges its footing on a submerged stone the current drags the cart off the ford's usual line into deeper water, soaking the grain sacks before anyone can pull it back onto course.

because: place is fed by rain upstream
numbers: how much higher and faster than the usual crossing

because: agent is familiar with the ford

numbers: how much sideways push at this depth and speed
how likely a misstep is on a hidden stone at this depth

effects: moves cart off the ford line
numbers: how far off course it is pushed
how much of the load is ruined

latent: a deep scour hole just off the ford's usual line, cut into the bed by this same overnight flood
state_after: ford: still passable, but changed since yesterday
cart: pushed off line, wheels in deep water
grain sacks: soaked
stress: a ford's safety is a property of the current water level and speed on that day, not a fixed label on the map
temptation: a rule that says fords are always safe, or that they close for a fixed number of hours after rain

place: A wide, slow stretch of the river frozen over after a hard frost, thick near the bank and untested further out.
lines: I walk out onto the ice near the bank to break a hole for water
I take a few more steps further out to see how it holds
outcome: The ice near the bank is thick enough to stand on, and breaking a hole there for water goes fine. Further out, where it's thinner, it gives way under the player's weight and drops them straight into the cold water beneath. The current running under the sheet pulls at them and makes climbing back onto the edge nearly impossible alone, and it takes a companion's rope and a hard pull to get them out, soaked and shaking.

numbers: how thick the ice is close to the bank
how many blows it takes to break through
how much weight the thin ice can bear at this distance out
how fast the cold saps strength
how much strength it takes to haul someone out over a slick edge

latent: a current running faster under the ice than on the surface, sweeping loose fragments of broken ice beneath the unbroken sheet
state_after: player: soaked, cold, on the bank, shaking
river ice: a hole near the bank, a wider break further out
companion: exhausted from the pull
stress: ice thickness varies by place and distance from shore, and the failure point is a threshold of load against thickness, not a flat safe or unsafe switch
temptation: a rule that says ice breaks after a fixed number of steps from the bank regardless of how thick it actually is

place: An old stone bridge pier standing in the main channel, where the current runs fastest against its upstream face.
outcome: Nobody does anything here; the fast water simply keeps scouring sand and gravel from around the base of the pier on its upstream side, over a long stretch of time deepening a hollow beneath the foundation stones. As the hollow grows, one side of the pier loses its footing and begins to lean, and eventually, most likely during the next high flow, enough support gives way at once that the pier settles hard and takes part of the bridge down with it.

because: place is narrowed by the pier
numbers: how deep the hollow becomes over months and years
how much support is lost as the hollow deepens
how much it tilts, and how fast
how high a flow it takes to trigger the final failure
how much of the bridge comes down

latent: a mason's inspection years ago that noted the same hollow forming, and was never acted on
state_after: bridge pier: leaning, undercut, part collapsed
bridge: missing a span
riverbed: a scoured hollow beneath where the pier stood
stress: gradual, invisible erosion beneath the waterline determines a structural failure that only looks sudden from above
temptation: a rule that says bridges collapse after a fixed number of years regardless of current speed or the ground beneath them

place: A raft lashed together from logs at a riverside camp, one of the logs having lain sunk in a still backwater for a whole season before being pulled out and used.
lines: I lash the logs together into a raft
I load the barrels on top and push off
outcome: Most of the logs float exactly as expected, but the one that soaked for a season in still water has taken on water all the way through and gives almost no lift. Lashed in among the others, it drags that corner of the raft low even before any load is added, and once the barrels go on, that corner dips under the surface. The raft tips enough that a barrel slides off the low side and is carried away.

numbers: how long submersion takes to fill the wood through
how much one waterlogged log drags a corner down
how much lower the already-low corner sits once loaded
at what added load the low corner goes under

effects: transfers barrel from raft to river water
numbers: how steep a tilt it takes before a barrel slides

latent: the waterlogged log was chosen for the raft because it looked identical to the dry ones from the outside
state_after: raft: tilted, one corner riding low, missing a barrel
waterlogged log: barely above the surface, most of it submerged
barrels: one afloat downstream or sunk depending on what it holds
stress: buoyancy is a property of how much water has already soaked into one specific log, invisible from the outside, not a fixed rule that wood floats
temptation: a rule that says rafts float unless overloaded by weight alone, ignoring what state the logs themselves are in

place: A stretch of fast water just below a bend, where the current runs strongest against the outer bank, a boat with two people aboard drifting through it.
lines: I lean out from the boat to grab the oar before it drifts away
I lose my footing and go in
outcome: Reaching too far for a lost oar tips the player's balance and pitches them into the fast water beside the boat. The current is stronger than it looked from the boat and pulls them under briefly before sweeping them downstream, and it is the companion throwing a rope from the boat, not swimming out after them, that finally gets them back aboard. Afterward the player is exhausted, chilled, and coughing up water, and the oar is gone for good.

numbers: how far out is too far to reach safely
how long the current holds them under
how far downstream before being reached
how far the throw has to reach
how much strength it takes to haul someone in against the current

latent: a stretch of even faster water just downstream, missed only because the rescue happened before reaching it
state_after: player: soaked, cold, coughing, exhausted
oar: lost downstream, never recovered
rope: wet and slack now
stress: rescue depends on a second person and a tool being at hand; the outcome would be very different if the player were alone
temptation: a rule that says falling in the river always ends in drowning, or that a thrown rope always saves whoever grabs it
